screens.title: Identity and Access Management (IAM) for Developers
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll build a clear mental model of AWS IAM as it applies to developers. IAM is how you safely grant credentials and permissions to your code, not just to people. You'll learn why roles and temporary credentials are central to secure applications, how policies express permissions, and how to avoid the common trap of overly broad access. For example, instead of embedding long-lived access keys in your code, attach a narrowly scoped role to a Lambda function so AWS injects temporary credentials automatically. That reduces risk from leaked keys and simplifies rotation. We'll also walk through a practical CLI workflow to create a role for a Lambda that reads an S3 bucket and writes to CloudWatch, then simulate the role locally to observe permitted and denied actions. By the end you should be able to decide when to use users, groups, or roles, author a basic policy with specific actions and ARNs, and interpret an AccessDenied error using CloudTrail and the IAM Policy Simulator. Think of IAM as rules that describe who can do what to which resource — and remember: always scope to the least privilege needed.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › IAM for Developers
Identity and Access Management (IAM)
Secure how code, services, and people access AWS. Focus on roles, policies, and temporary credentials.
Why this matters
Application identities must be managed securely to prevent unauthorized access and data leakage.
Practical focus
Roles for EC2 and Lambda, temporary credentials, and policy scoping are the core developer touchpoints.
In this lesson: create a role for Lambda, attach a least-privilege policy, simulate assume-role, and diagnose AccessDenied with CloudTrail and the Policy Simulator.
Explore Key Topics
Roles & Temp Creds
How AWS provides short-lived credentials to running code.
Policies
Identity vs resource policies and scoping to ARNs and actions.
Troubleshooting
Using CloudTrail and the Policy Simulator to fix AccessDenied errors.
Concept Map
IAM Role
Assumed by services to receive temporary credentials.
Policy
JSON that allows or denies specific actions on resources.
Instance Profile
A container that attaches a role to EC2 instances.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will reliably reason about IAM, select the correct identity type for an application, and create narrowly scoped policies. First, you will understand core IAM principles and why the principle of least privilege is the foundation of secure design. Second, you'll be able to distinguish users, groups, and roles and pick roles for running code. Third, you will implement roles for EC2 and Lambda, including how instance profiles connect a role to an EC2 instance. Fourth, you'll use temporary credentials via the AWS SDK and learn how to simulate and troubleshoot permissions with CloudTrail and the IAM Policy Simulator. Each objective maps directly to a developer workflow: author a policy that grants s3:GetObject on a single bucket, attach it to a role, and verify from the running environment. Practically, this helps you avoid long-lived access keys, reduce blast radius if credentials are compromised, and maintain auditable permission changes. We will practice creating a Lambda role and testing allowed and denied S3 operations in the hands-on segment so you can apply these objectives in real projects.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Developer Workflows
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives translate directly into developer actions you'll perform in the workflow. Understand IAM so you can confidently decide whether to add a user, place someone into a group, or create a role for running code. Implementing roles and instance profiles is a basic operational task: attach a role to EC2 or configure a Lambda execution role rather than shipping keys. Use temporary credentials provided by the AWS SDK, so your application automatically receives rotated keys. When an AccessDenied appears, you'll check the role's identity-based policy, then inspect CloudTrail to find the denied A P I call and principal. Finally, use the IAM Policy Simulator to validate that your intended policy grants the exact permissions required. Practically, this reduces incidents caused by leaked credentials and makes audits and least-privilege reviews easier. We'll practice the create, attach, simulate loop in the hands-on activity so you can both apply and verify these objectives in a safe test environment.

screens.title: What is IAM and the Principle of Least Privilege
screens.narratorSegment: IAM is the service that controls who can do what to which AWS resources. For developers, the most important mental model is that identities represent principals and policies describe allowed or denied actions. The principle of least privilege means granting only the minimal set of permissions necessary for a task. Practically, that reduces exposure when a credential is compromised. A concrete example: a Lambda that reads user profile images should have s3:GetObject for the specific bucket path only, not s3:* on every bucket. A common misconception is to treat IAM as only for humans; instead, treat it as the fabric that ties services and code to permissions. Roles, not users, should be used for running code because roles yield temporary credentials and avoid long-lived keys. When authoring policies, prefer action-level scoping such as s3:GetObject and explicit resource ARNs. Remember that overly broad policies are often used as a shortcut during development; they create technical debt and security risk in production. A closing question to reflect on: if an attacker gained the Lambda execution role, what resources would they access with the current policy, and how would you reduce that surface?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: IAM = identities + policies. Least privilege limits permissions to reduce risk.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › What is IAM
IAM & Least Privilege
Define identities and policies; grant minimal permissions.
Core claim
IAM ties principals to permissions via policies. For running code use roles to get temporary credentials.
Concrete example
A Lambda should have s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/* rather than s3:* on all buckets.
Common misconception
Giving broad permissions to simplify development is dangerous; it inflates blast radius when keys are leaked.
Key Takeaway

Treat roles as the primary identity for running code and grant only the actions and resources required.

Analogy: Keys to rooms
Policies are like access rules that say which rooms a key can open. Roles hand out temporary keys that expire.
Policy snippet (illustrative)
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*"
}
Check your understanding
  • List the minimal actions your code needs.
  • Restrict resources to specific ARNs when possible.
  • Avoid embedding long-lived access keys in code.

screens.title: IAM Identities: Users, Groups, Roles
screens.narratorSegment: Developers must know when to use an IAM user, group, or role. An IAM user is an identity for a person or a service that needs long-lived credentials; it's typical for console access or programmatic access with access keys. A group is a collection of users that lets you manage permissions for many people at once — for example, a developers group with permissions to common resources. An IAM role is a different construct: it is assumed by trusted principals such as EC2 instances, Lambda functions, or an external identity provider and yields temporary security credentials. Roles are the recommended mechanism for running code because AWS manages credential rotation. For instance, attach a role to a Lambda to grant s3:GetObject on a specific bucket; the function will automatically use temporary credentials supplied by the execution environment. A common mistake is creating users and embedding their access keys into application configuration. That creates long-lived secrets and increases risk. Contrast this with roles: if a role is compromised, credentials are short-lived and automatically rotated, reducing exposure. Consider this quick decision rule: humans = users and groups; running code or federated identities = roles.

keyIdea.title: Identity comparison
keyIdea.text: Users for humans, groups to manage users, roles for services and temporary credentials.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Users vs Groups vs Roles
Identity Types
Choose the identity type that matches the principal.
IAM User
Identity for an individual or service that needs long-lived credentials for direct interaction.
Use for console access; avoid for running applications.
IAM Group
Manage permissions for multiple users. Attach policies to the group to grant the same permissions to all members.
IAM Role
Assumed by compute or federated principals to receive temporary credentials; preferred for running code.
Key Takeaway

Assign roles to running services; use users for humans and groups to simplify user permission management.

Decision rule
Humans use users and groups. Services and code use roles with scoped policies and temporary credentials.
Example
A web app running on EC2 needs to write to S3 and publish to SQS: create a role with s3:PutObject and sqs:SendMessage for the specific resources, then attach via an instance profile.
Common mistake
Embedding a developer IAM user's access keys into application config. That creates long-lived secrets and is insecure.
Check your understanding
  • When would you prefer a role over a user?
  • How would you group developers with similar console permissions?

screens.title: How Policies Work: Identity-based vs Resource-based
screens.narratorSegment: Policies are JSON documents that grant or deny actions on resources. There are two categories you must know: identity-based policies and resource-based policies. Identity-based policies attach to users, groups, or roles and say what that identity can do. Resource-based policies attach directly to a resource, like an S3 bucket or SQS queue, and specify which principals can access that resource. Both can be combined to produce the effective permission. For a Lambda that invokes another Lambda, the caller needs permission via its identity-based policy and the callee may require a resource-based (permissions) policy to allow that principal to invoke it. When writing policies, use specific action names such as s3:GetObject instead of s3:* and specify resource ARNs rather than using wildcards. A common troubleshooting pitfall is forgetting to set the trust policy for a role; the role must allow the desired service principal to assume it. To validate policies before deployment, use the IAM Policy Simulator to ensure the intended actions are allowed and nothing extra is granted. Reflect: which resource would you limit first when tightening a broad policy?

keyIdea.title: Policy types
keyIdea.text: Identity-based policies attach to principals; resource-based policies attach to resources. Both affect effective permissions.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Policies
Identity-based vs Resource-based
How attaching a policy to a principal differs from attaching it to a resource.
Identity-based policy
Attached to a user, group or role; controls what the principal can do across resources.
Resource-based policy
Attached to a resource and allows principals to access that resource directly.
Trust policy
A role's trust policy defines who can assume the role. Without it assume-role calls will fail.
Pro tip

Test the outcome with the IAM Policy Simulator and check CloudTrail when you see unexpected AccessDenied events.

Example scenario
Caller role has lambda:InvokeFunction allowed, but the target Lambda also needs a resource-based permission for that principal. Missing resource policy produces an AccessDenied on invoke.
Check-list
  • Confirm identity-based policy grants the needed action.
  • If invoking another resource, check its resource-based policy.
  • Validate the role trust policy allows the intended principal.
Why it matters
Combining these policy types controls the precise access behavior of your application and reduces accidental open access.
Key Takeaway

Both policy types matter; check identity, resource, and trust policies when diagnosing permissions.

screens.title: Roles for EC2 and Instance Profiles
screens.narratorSegment: When you run applications on EC2, you should avoid configuring access keys on the instance. Instead, use an instance profile that contains an IAM role. The instance profile is a container that the EC2 service uses to provide a role to the instance; applications on the instance then obtain temporary credentials from the instance metadata service. This flow means your code can use the AWS SDK without embedding keys: the SDK automatically queries metadata, receives short-lived keys, and refreshes them as needed. A concrete example: an EC2-based worker uploads files to a specific S3 bucket. You create a role with s3:PutObject on that bucket, create an instance profile for the role, and attach it to the EC2 instance. The application uses the AWS SDK to call the upload A P I and the SDK fetches temporary credentials transparently. A misconception to avoid is thinking instance profile names are the role — the profile contains the role. For security, scope the role's policy to exact ARNs and actions, and avoid attaching overly broad managed policies. Reflect: how would you rotate permissions if the worker later needs read-only access too?

keyIdea.title: Instance profile flow
keyIdea.text: Attach a role to EC2 via an instance profile so SDKs can automatically retrieve temporary credentials.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Instance Profiles
EC2 Roles and Instance Profiles
How to provide credentials to software running on an EC2 instance.
Flow
  1. Create role with policies for required actions.
  2. Create instance profile containing the role.
  3. Attach profile to EC2 instance; SDK reads credentials from metadata.
Concrete example
Worker on EC2 needs s3:PutObject on my-app-uploads; role policy grants only that action to the specific bucket ARN.
Misconception
Don't assume instance profile equals role name. The profile is a container linking a role to an instance.
Key Takeaway

Use instance profiles to safely provide temporary credentials to EC2; scope policies tightly.

Developer checklist
  • Create a role with precise S3 and SQS actions.
  • Create and attach an instance profile to your EC2 instance.
  • Verify your application retrieves temporary credentials via the SDK.
Why it matters
Automatic credential rotation removes the burden of managing secret keys on instances and reduces risk from leaked credentials.

screens.title: Lambda Execution Role and Temporary Credentials
screens.narratorSegment: Lambda functions should be given an execution role rather than embedding credentials. When you attach a role to a Lambda, AWS provides temporary security credentials to the function's runtime. The AWS SDK inside the function picks up these credentials from the environment automatically. This means the code simply calls the SDK client and the environment supplies short-lived access key ID, secret access key, and session token. A concrete example: configure a Lambda role with s3:GetObject on a bucket and logs:PutLogEvents for CloudWatch. The Lambda will be able to read S3 objects and write logs without any credential handling in source code. A common error is granting too-broad permissions to get things working; instead, grant explicit actions and limited ARNs. Another potential pitfall is forgetting to attach the role when creating or updating the function, which results in runtime failures. Finally, remember to audit roles periodically and remove unused permissions. Reflection: if a function needs to call other AWS services, list each required action first and restrict each to the minimal ARN possible. Lambda Execution Role and Temporary Credentials means attach an execution role to lambda so the runtime receives temporary credentials; sdks use them transparently.. In practical terms, how lambda receives credentials and how the sdk uses them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lambda roles
keyIdea.text: Attach an execution role to Lambda so the runtime receives temporary credentials; SDKs use them transparently.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Lambda Execution Role
Lambda's Temporary Credentials
The runtime receives short-lived credentials from AWS when a role is attached.
How it works
Attach an execution role; AWS injects temporary keys into the runtime environment; SDKs fetch and refresh them automatically.
Concrete policy example
Grant s3:GetObject for a specific bucket and CloudWatch Logs write permissions for logging.
Key Takeaway

Prefer execution roles for Lambda; avoid embedding access keys inside function code.

Example: Required permissions
For reading S3 and logging, include s3:GetObject on the bucket ARN and logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream, logs:PutLogEvents on CloudWatch Logs.
Developer checklist
  • Create the role with a correct trust policy for lambda.amazonaws.com.
  • Attach a policy limited to needed actions and resources.
  • Associate the role when you configure the function.
Pitfall
Forgetting trust policy entries prevents the role from being assumed. Ensure the role's trust policy lists the Lambda service principal.

screens.title: Create a Lambda Role: CLI Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the practical CLI commands to create a role for Lambda. First you author a trust policy that allows the Lambda service to assume the role. Next you create an identity policy granting s3:GetObject on your specific bucket and CloudWatch Logs permissions. Then create the role, attach the inline policy, and note the role ARN. This process avoids placing keys in code and results in temporary credentials being injected at runtime. A concrete example from the chapter shows the trust policy JSON and the permission policy JSON. When you run aws iam create-role and aws iam put-role-policy, note the returned role ARN which you will use when configuring the Lambda. A typical local test uses sts assume-role to simulate the credentials that Lambda would receive. Remember to update ARNs to your bucket name and account id; hardcoding wildcards like * defeats least privilege. Finally, clean up test resources after validation to reduce unused permissions. How would you adapt the policy if the function later needed to list a bucket instead of reading objects? Create a Lambda Role: CLI Walkthrough means create role with a trust policy, attach a scoped identity policy, then configure the lambda to use that role.. In practical terms, hands-on commands to create trust and permission policies and attach them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Create role with a trust policy, attach a scoped identity policy, then configure the Lambda to use that role.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › CLI Walkthrough
Create role and attach policies
Sample trust and permission policy snippets you will use.
Trust policy (lambda-trust-policy.json)
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "Service": "lambda.amazonaws.com" },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}
Permission policy (lambda-s3-read-policy.json)
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::cohortia-dev-app-data-YOURNAME/*" },
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["logs:CreateLogGroup","logs:CreateLogStream","logs:PutLogEvents"], "Resource": "arn:aws:logs:*:*:*" }
  ]
}

screens.narratorSegment: Simulating assume-role locally helps you confirm the effective permissions a role grants. Module 07 › Chapter 7.1 › Simulate Assume-Role
Simulate credentials
Capture and export temporary credentials so you can run the same commands your function runs.
# Assume the role locally
ROLE_ARN="arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/CohortiaLambdaS3ReaderRole"
TEMP=$(aws sts assume-role --role-arn $ROLE_ARN --role-session-name TestSession --duration-seconds 900)
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(echo $TEMP | jq -r '.Credentials.AccessKeyId')
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(echo $TEMP | jq -r '.Credentials.SecretAccessKey')
export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=$(echo $TEMP | jq -r '.Credentials.SessionToken')

# Test read (should succeed)
aws s3 cp s3://cohortia-dev-app-data-YOURNAME/test_data.txt ./downloaded.txt

# Test write (should fail with AccessDenied)
echo "unauthorized" > bad.txt
aws s3 cp bad.txt s3://cohortia-dev-app-data-YOURNAME/bad.txt

# Clean up
unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN
Troubleshoot

If an allowed action fails, inspect the role policy and CloudTrail to find which statement denied the API call.

Interpreting results
  • Success on read: the policy allows s3:GetObject for that ARN.
  • Failure on write: the policy lacks s3:PutObject; expected AccessDenied confirms least-privilege.
  • Unexpected write success: search for wildcards or broader policies attached to the role.
CloudTrail check
Use CloudTrail logs to see the denied API call, which principal attempted it, and the policy decision for rapid investigation.

screens.narratorSegment: When your application reports AccessDenied, follow a reproducible troubleshooting flow. First, identify the principal: which role or user attempted the action. Next, find the exact A P I call in CloudTrail; CloudTrail records the call, the principal, the caller's ARN, and the error. With the A P I call in hand, use the IAM Policy Simulator to test the principal's policies against the specific action and resource. The simulator will show which statement denied or allowed the call, helping you refine the policy without repeatedly deploying changes. If invoking another resource, remember to check that resource's resource-based policy; for example, invoking a Lambda often requires a permission on the target function as well. A common oversight is trusting that the execution role's policy alone governs access — resource policies and trust policies can also block an action. After making a targeted policy change, rerun the same A P I call in a safe test to confirm the fix and then log the change for audit. This disciplined approach reduces guesswork and limits permission creep. screens.title: Common IAM Misconfigurations and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Developers often take shortcuts that lead to misconfigurations. The most common errors are: using wildcard actions or resources (for example s3:* on *), embedding long-lived access keys in code, forgetting trust policies for roles, and neglecting to scope policies to specific ARNs. Each of these mistakes increases the attack surface. Safer alternatives are straightforward: follow the principle of least privilege by listing only required actions, specify exact ARNs for resources, prefer roles for compute so credentials are temporary, and use the IAM Policy Simulator and CloudTrail to validate and audit permissions. A concrete case: a developer uses s3:* to make testing faster; when deployed to production that permission can allow deletion or listing of unrelated buckets. Instead, identify exactly which A P I calls are needed, for example s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on a single bucket path, then test those operations. Another useful practice is periodic permission review — remove unused permissions and document why a permission exists. A closing question: what routine would you add to your deployment checklist to prevent accidental wildcard permissions? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a clear mental model of AWS IAM as it applies to developers. IAM is how you safely grant credentials and permissions to your code, not just to people. You'll learn why roles and temporary credentials are central to secure applications, how policies express permissions, and how to avoid the common trap of overly broad access. For example, instead of embedding long-lived access keys in your code, attach a narrowly scoped role to a Lambda function so AWS injects temporary credentials automatically. That reduces risk from leaked keys and simplifies rotation. We'll also walk through a practical CLI workflow to create a role for a Lambda that reads an S3 bucket and writes to CloudWatch, then simulate the role locally to observe permitted and denied actions. By the end you should be able to decide when to use users, groups, or roles, author a basic policy with specific actions and ARNs, and interpret an AccessDenied error using CloudTrail and the IAM Policy Simulator. Think of IAM as rules that describe who can do what to which resource — and remember: always scope to the least privilege needed.

By the end of this chapter you will reliably reason about IAM, select the correct identity type for an application, and create narrowly scoped policies. First, you will understand core IAM principles and why the principle of least privilege is the foundation of secure design. Second, you'll be able to distinguish users, groups, and roles and pick roles for running code. Third, you will implement roles for EC2 and Lambda, including how instance profiles connect a role to an EC2 instance. Fourth, you'll use temporary credentials via the AWS SDK and learn how to simulate and troubleshoot permissions with CloudTrail and the IAM Policy Simulator. Each objective maps directly to a developer workflow: author a policy that grants s3:GetObject on a single bucket, attach it to a role, and verify from the running environment. Practically, this helps you avoid long-lived access keys, reduce blast radius if credentials are compromised, and maintain auditable permission changes. We will practice creating a Lambda role and testing allowed and denied S3 operations in the hands-on segment so you can apply these objectives in real projects.

These objectives translate directly into developer actions you'll perform in the workflow. Understand IAM so you can confidently decide whether to add a user, place someone into a group, or create a role for running code. Implementing roles and instance profiles is a basic operational task: attach a role to EC2 or configure a Lambda execution role rather than shipping keys. Use temporary credentials provided by the AWS SDK, so your application automatically receives rotated keys. When an AccessDenied appears, you'll check the role's identity-based policy, then inspect CloudTrail to find the denied A P I call and principal. Finally, use the IAM Policy Simulator to validate that your intended policy grants the exact permissions required. Practically, this reduces incidents caused by leaked credentials and makes audits and least-privilege reviews easier. We'll practice the create, attach, simulate loop in the hands-on activity so you can both apply and verify these objectives in a safe test environment.

IAM is the service that controls who can do what to which AWS resources. For developers, the most important mental model is that identities represent principals and policies describe allowed or denied actions. The principle of least privilege means granting only the minimal set of permissions necessary for a task. Practically, that reduces exposure when a credential is compromised. A concrete example: a Lambda that reads user profile images should have s3:GetObject for the specific bucket path only, not s3:* on every bucket. A common misconception is to treat IAM as only for humans; instead, treat it as the fabric that ties services and code to permissions. Roles, not users, should be used for running code because roles yield temporary credentials and avoid long-lived keys. When authoring policies, prefer action-level scoping such as s3:GetObject and explicit resource ARNs. Remember that overly broad policies are often used as a shortcut during development; they create technical debt and security risk in production. A closing question to reflect on: if an attacker gained the Lambda execution role, what resources would they access with the current policy, and how would you reduce that surface?

Developers must know when to use an IAM user, group, or role. An IAM user is an identity for a person or a service that needs long-lived credentials; it's typical for console access or programmatic access with access keys. A group is a collection of users that lets you manage permissions for many people at once — for example, a developers group with permissions to common resources. An IAM role is a different construct: it is assumed by trusted principals such as EC2 instances, Lambda functions, or an external identity provider and yields temporary security credentials. Roles are the recommended mechanism for running code because AWS manages credential rotation. For instance, attach a role to a Lambda to grant s3:GetObject on a specific bucket; the function will automatically use temporary credentials supplied by the execution environment. A common mistake is creating users and embedding their access keys into application configuration. That creates long-lived secrets and increases risk. Contrast this with roles: if a role is compromised, credentials are short-lived and automatically rotated, reducing exposure. Consider this quick decision rule: humans = users and groups; running code or federated identities = roles.

Policies are JSON documents that grant or deny actions on resources. There are two categories you must know: identity-based policies and resource-based policies. Identity-based policies attach to users, groups, or roles and say what that identity can do. Resource-based policies attach directly to a resource, like an S3 bucket or SQS queue, and specify which principals can access that resource. Both can be combined to produce the effective permission. For a Lambda that invokes another Lambda, the caller needs permission via its identity-based policy and the callee may require a resource-based (permissions) policy to allow that principal to invoke it. When writing policies, use specific action names such as s3:GetObject instead of s3:* and specify resource ARNs rather than using wildcards. A common troubleshooting pitfall is forgetting to set the trust policy for a role; the role must allow the desired service principal to assume it. To validate policies before deployment, use the IAM Policy Simulator to ensure the intended actions are allowed and nothing extra is granted. Reflect: which resource would you limit first when tightening a broad policy?

When you run applications on EC2, you should avoid configuring access keys on the instance. Instead, use an instance profile that contains an IAM role. The instance profile is a container that the EC2 service uses to provide a role to the instance; applications on the instance then obtain temporary credentials from the instance metadata service. This flow means your code can use the AWS SDK without embedding keys: the SDK automatically queries metadata, receives short-lived keys, and refreshes them as needed. A concrete example: an EC2-based worker uploads files to a specific S3 bucket. You create a role with s3:PutObject on that bucket, create an instance profile for the role, and attach it to the EC2 instance. The application uses the AWS SDK to call the upload A P I and the SDK fetches temporary credentials transparently. A misconception to avoid is thinking instance profile names are the role — the profile contains the role. For security, scope the role's policy to exact ARNs and actions, and avoid attaching overly broad managed policies. Reflect: how would you rotate permissions if the worker later needs read-only access too?

Lambda functions should be given an execution role rather than embedding credentials. When you attach a role to a Lambda, AWS provides temporary security credentials to the function's runtime. The AWS SDK inside the function picks up these credentials from the environment automatically. This means the code simply calls the SDK client and the environment supplies short-lived access key ID, secret access key, and session token. A concrete example: configure a Lambda role with s3:GetObject on a bucket and logs:PutLogEvents for CloudWatch. The Lambda will be able to read S3 objects and write logs without any credential handling in source code. A common error is granting too-broad permissions to get things working; instead, grant explicit actions and limited ARNs. Another potential pitfall is forgetting to attach the role when creating or updating the function, which results in runtime failures. Finally, remember to audit roles periodically and remove unused permissions. Reflection: if a function needs to call other AWS services, list each required action first and restrict each to the minimal ARN possible. Lambda Execution Role and Temporary Credentials means attach an execution role to lambda so the runtime receives temporary credentials; sdks use them transparently.. In practical terms, how lambda receives credentials and how the sdk uses them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the practical CLI commands to create a role for Lambda. First you author a trust policy that allows the Lambda service to assume the role. Next you create an identity policy granting s3:GetObject on your specific bucket and CloudWatch Logs permissions. Then create the role, attach the inline policy, and note the role ARN. Developers often take shortcuts that lead to misconfigurations. The most common errors are: using wildcard actions or resources (for example s3:* on *), embedding long-lived access keys in code, forgetting trust policies for roles, and neglecting to scope policies to specific ARNs. Each of these mistakes increases the attack surface. Safer alternatives are straightforward: follow the principle of least privilege by listing only required actions, specify exact ARNs for resources, prefer roles for compute so credentials are temporary, and use the IAM Policy Simulator and CloudTrail to validate and audit permissions. A concrete case: a developer uses s3:* to make testing faster; when deployed to production that permission can allow deletion or listing of unrelated buckets. Instead, identify exactly which A P I calls are needed, for example s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on a single bucket path, then test those operations. Another useful practice is periodic permission review — remove unused permissions and document why a permission exists. These concise concept cards summarize the essential points developers must retain. First, IAM Role: a principal that services assume to receive temporary credentials, and it is the preferred identity for running code. Second, IAM Policy: a JSON document that defines allowed or denied actions on specific resources — always scope policies to the minimum required actions and resource ARNs. Third, Principle of Least Privilege: a guiding security rule: grant only what is necessary. Keep these three concepts in mind when designing access for applications, and use the Policy Simulator and CloudTrail to validate and troubleshoot permissions. As a practical habit, avoid embedding long-lived access keys, attach roles to compute resources, and review policies periodically.
